primary.thesis: Going into the October 27, 2026 election, the coalition that has governed since 2022 looks damaged. It carries the October 7 failure, the fight over drafting Haredi men into the army, the judicial-overhaul split and a long war. Recent polls have put the opposition, with Naftali Bennett's new list as its biggest party, ahead of Netanyahu's right-wing and religious bloc. My view is that Netanyahu's bloc falls short of 61 seats. The President then gives Bennett the mandate to form a government, as leader of the largest opposition list. He builds a coalition with Eizenkot, Lapid, Lieberman, Gantz and Golan, possibly relying on outside support or abstentions from some Haredi or Arab members. Bennett is sworn in first under any rotation deal, well before the December 31, 2027 deadline.

basket.reason: Bennett leads the largest opposition list and is the most likely person to head an anti-Netanyahu coalition. Any rotation deal would very probably put him first, as happened in 2021.

This pays out in two different worlds. In one, the opposition forms a government. In the other, there is a deadlock and a repeat election, Netanyahu stays only as caretaker, and caretakers do not count. It also pays if someone else in Likud replaces him. It loses only if Netanyahu himself forms a government and is sworn in.

failure_narrative: Netanyahu's bloc gets to 61 seats. That could happen through a rally-around-the-flag effect, anti-Arab-party messaging, or opposition votes wasted on lists below the threshold (Yisrael Beiteinu-style or small left-wing lists falling under 3.25%). Or the opposition falls apart in coalition talks: Lieberman won't sit with the Haredim, the Arab parties are ruled out, and Bennett won't rely on Ra'am. Netanyahu then brings in a defector such as Gantz or a Haredi-friendly faction and is sworn in again. C1 NO and C2 YES both lose. A smaller failure: the opposition does form a government, but it is headed by Eizenkot or Lapid instead of Bennett.
hedge_thesis: If Netanyahu is sworn in again, Israel keeps on its current course: continued military pressure on Gaza, Lebanon and Iran, a bigger chance of annexation steps in the West Bank, the judicial overhaul coming back, and Saudi normalization stalled. That raises the geopolitical and institutional risk priced into Israeli assets and the region. The shekel would likely weaken, Israeli sovereign credit spreads and CDS would widen, and TA-35 banks would lag Israeli defense names such as Elbit. Gulf and Iran tension would keep a risk premium in Brent crude. These are the same worlds where the Bennett-long, Netanyahu-short basket loses. An opposition win would tend to push each of these the other way.
